record.paper_title: Open Problems in Communication and Computation
record.original_question: Is there a mathematically meaningful notion of energy-free computation, and if so, where do information theory, communication theory, computer science, and physics meet at the atomic level?

evidence.quote: Is there a notion of energy-free computation? And if so, where do information theory, communication theory, computer science, and physics meet at the atomic level?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Formulate a mathematically rigorous notion of "energy-free computation," i.e., a model of computation in which the execution of an arbitrary computable function (or some suitably large class of computational tasks) can be carried out with zero net energy dissipation, and determine whether such a notion can exist in a meaningful sense. More precisely:

(a) Provide a mathematical framework that unifies the basic objects of information theory (entropy, mutual information, channel capacity), communication theory (encoding, decoding, noise), computer science (computational steps, logical states, reversibility), and physics at the atomic/quantum scale (Hamiltonian dynamics, thermodynamic entropy, Landauer's bound k_B T ln 2 per bit erasure), in which one can speak unambiguously of the energy cost of performing a computation.

(b) Within this framework, decide whether there exists a model of computation, possibly using logically reversible operations or quantum-mechanical evolution, that can perform a universal class of computations with arbitrarily small (or exactly zero) total energy dissipation per logical operation, taking into account the cost of initialization, readout, error correction, and interaction with any environment.

(c) Identify and characterize the precise mathematical meeting point of information theory, communication theory, computability/complexity, and physical law at the atomic scale: state the fundamental laws (analogous to Shannon's channel coding theorem and Landauer's principle) that govern this meeting point, and prove or disprove the existence of an energy-free universal computer.
artifact.status_search_result: The question of whether truly energy-free (zero-dissipation) universal computation is achievable remains an active foundational problem at the interface of information theory, computer science, and physics. Landauer's principle (1961) gives a lower bound k_B T ln 2 per irreversible bit erasure, and reversible/quantum computing is the candidate route to circumvent it, but recent work (e.g., 2021 "Quantum Foundations of Classical Reversible Computing" and a 2025 arXiv survey on Landauer's principle and thermodynamics of computation) shows that the precise relationship between logical and thermodynamic reversibility, and the engineering/mathematical feasibility of arbitrarily-low-energy universal computation, are still under investigation and not settled.

status_evidence.title: Landauer's principle - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: It is hypothesized that energy consumption below the Landauer bound would require the development of reversible computing.
status_evidence.claim: Achieving energy use below Landauer's bound is still hypothesized to require reversible computing and is not yet realized.

status_evidence.title: Landauer Principle and Thermodynamics of Computation
status_evidence.snippet: Recent survey on Landauer principle and thermodynamics of computation (2025).
status_evidence.claim: The thermodynamics of computation remains an active research area as of 2025.

status_evidence.title: Quantum Foundations of Classical Reversible Computing
status_evidence.snippet: Recent advances in non-equilibrium statistical physics have established that there is not a prior relationship between logical and thermodynamic reversibility.
status_evidence.claim: The mathematical relationship between logical reversibility and energy-free computation is still being clarified.
